## The Leftovers (2014–2017)

Few television series have asked bigger questions than The Leftovers. After two percent of the world’s population mysteriously disappears without explanation, the HBO drama spends three seasons exploring grief, faith, guilt, and humanity’s search for meaning rather than trying to solve the mystery itself. The finale understands that some questions matter less than the people searching for the answers.

Why it worked

The ending succeeds because it remains completely faithful to the show’s central philosophy. The Leftovers was never interested in providing scientific explanations or neatly tying together every mystery. Instead, it focused on how people cope when life refuses to make sense. [...] ## The Good Place (2016–2020)

Comedy series rarely end by asking viewers to reflect on the meaning of existence, yet that’s exactly what The Good Place accomplished. Over four inventive seasons, the sitcom evolved from a clever afterlife comedy into a thoughtful exploration of ethics, friendship, and what gives life purpose. Its finale, “Whenever You’re Ready,” managed to answer those enormous questions while remaining warm, funny, and deeply human.

Why it worked [...] Its lasting legacy

The finale earned widespread acclaim for resisting the temptation to become an action spectacle. Instead, it trusted viewers to appreciate an ending driven by character and emotional truth. Critics frequently cite it as one of the finest conclusions of the modern television era, praising its restraint and willingness to accept that not every story can end happily. Like the series itself, the finale proves that the greatest tension often comes not from bullets or explosions, but from the choices people make when there are no good options left.

Where to watch: Available to stream; sold on physical media and digitally.

## I want to end by talking about Rookie. It's been a couple of months since the book came out. What was it like seeing the massive reaction to such a personal work?

Joshua: If somebody comes up to me on the street and says that Rookie changed their life, I just start sobbing, like, instantly. I don't know what it is about people resonating with Rookie that just makes me sob. [...] When the Knicks won, I remember walking down the street, and people were breaking bottles, and everyone was screaming — and it didn't faze me at all. I was thinking, "Dude, me a year ago, when I just got back to New York, would've been freaking the fuck out right now." I literally was just walking around, and no part of me was stressed or overwhelmed. It was just life.

When I have friends visit, it's funny just watching them experience New York and, like, not knowing how to cross the street properly.

Silhouette of a person looking at the sky, with the text "joshua bassett clouds" on the left

That's just the way it works for me. A lot of times, artists have these spurts of flow-state moments, where you can go three hours without anything, and then all of a sudden you write an entire verse in two minutes. My practice is: How do you stretch out and keep tapping into that flow state for as long as possible?

I worked on almost every song with Nate Miles. He's so good at knowing when to just hit record when I'm not paying attention. I'll be sitting at the piano, and he'll just toss me headphones, and then I'll be walking around trying to finish the verse. I'll go to a synth, start experimenting, and just kind of throw it in.

Naomi Scott’s F.I.G was my big surprise of the year—partly because I had no idea that Scott, who you might remember from her starring roles in Aladdin and Smile 2, even made music. On her impressively self-assured and seriously stylish debut album, she merges R&B, alt-pop, and soul to create a sophisticated but also idiosyncratic sonic self-portrait of a “girl in process,” as she said when I spoke to her for a story in June. I can’t remember exactly how I stumbled upon it, but it ended up being one of those records that I can listen to in any place, at any time, and it has serious replay value. (I wouldn’t be surprised if it ended up in the number one spot on my Spotify Wrapped.) I dare you to find a more irresistible chorus than “Cherry” or a groovier bassline than “Gracie” on any other [...] ## Glaive and Kurtains, God Save The Three

One thing you notice right away is there is a lot of singing on electronic artist glaive’s latest album with his friend and collaborator kurtains. There are beats too, the ominous trap-influenced rhythms glaive has specialized in on his excellent recent releases (Y’all and May It Never Falter), but the mood on this album is softer, affectionate and upbeat, with ballad-y interludes of acoustic guitar and piano. The whole thing is a paean to friendship, unexpected success, and partying. Standouts are “The Front,” “The Band,” “Let’s Link Up and Die,” but head straight for “The Troubles,” the album’s out-and-out banger with its jubilant refrain: “We get money, like the Troubles, blow it at the mall.” —Taylor Antrim

## Good Sleepy, Constant Humming [...] Though Arca hasn’t released a record in nearly five years, she’s continued to contribute to the pop music lexicon, most recently with her take on Addison Rae’s “Aquamarine”—“Arcamarine.” So when news of her latest album, XXXXX, arrived with no singles, I had no idea what to expect. Her previous releases, kick i–iii, a three-part trilogy, gave us everything from reggaeton/neoperreo to improvised piano tracks. From the opening track of XXXXX, “No End,” I was excited to hear Arca return to her roots: hard-hitting experimental electronic dance music. Few artists can make dance music that makes you want to think as much as it makes you want to move, and this record does exactly that. There are plenty of clicky percussion sounds, playful saw-wave synths, and Arca’s signature approach to sound

“A Reunion of Old Friends” brings together four longtime friends and colleagues in a program spanning the Romantic era and beyond. Griffitt, Bedelian and Edberg will perform Clara Schumann’s "Piano Trio," while Griffitt and Edberg will share the slow movement of a work by Sergei Rachmaninoff. Griffitt and Cymerman will perform movements from Georges Bizet’s “Jeux d’enfants,” a transcription of the famous “Habanera” from Carmen, and conclude with Wendy Hiscocks’ transcription of Camille Saint-Saëns’ “Danse macabre.”

The program brings together intimate chamber music, familiar melodies and virtuosic arrangements as the festival celebrates the friendships and musical connections at the heart of its final concert of the summer. [...] Edberg, founding artistic director of the Greencastle Summer Music Festival, is a classical and improvising cellist dedicated to connecting and enlivening others through music. A concerto soloist, recitalist and chamber musician, he has performed internationally as well as in nursing homes, schools, hospitals, prisons and the New York City subways. Edberg is professor of music emeritus at DePauw, where his work teaching improvisation was featured in The Wall Street Journal.

As the final concert of the 2026 summer season, “A Reunion of Old Friends” celebrates not only the music on the program, but also the friendships and collaborations that have connected these musicians across the years.

Burna Boy

His biggest formal milestone came with “Twice as Tall,” which won the Grammy for Best Global Music Album at the 2021 Grammy Awards. That victory made Burna Boy the first Nigerian artiste to win the category under its current name, adding a major international award to a catalogue that had already established him as one of Africa’s leading performers. The Recording Academy continues to list Burna Boy among Grammy recognised artistes, with nominations extending into 2026. [...] 2baba also made history at the MTV Europe Music Awards in 2005 when he won Best African Act. The award was particularly significant because he became the first winner of the category, placing a Nigerian artiste at the forefront of an international award platform during a period when African pop music had not yet reached its current level of global visibility. His catalogue therefore carries something Davido’s younger generation cannot fully replicate, which is the ability to measure a song’s influence across a much longer stretch of Nigerian music history.

### Psquare’s Continental Dominance [...] That leaves the door open for the story to develop further. If Davido responds directly to Portable, the conversation could become more specific. If another major artiste enters the challenge, the comparison could become even larger. For now, however, the facts are straightforward: Davido has put $1 million behind his confidence, Portable has claimed he has more hits, and the careers of Wizkid, Burna Boy, Olamide, 2baba, Psquare and Kizz Daniel provide enough documented achievements to show why this is one of the biggest catalogue debates Nigerian music can produce.

## Plot

Cleopatra (1963)

The film traces the romances between the Egyptian queen Cleopatra (played by Taylor) and her Roman suitors Julius Caesar (Rex Harrison) and Mark Antony (Burton). Caesar, infatuated with the beautiful Cleopatra, declares her sole ruler over Egypt, although he keeps her as his own lover. When Caesar is assassinated in Rome, Antony, his protégé, assumes power, and he too becomes obsessed with Cleopatra. He eventually marries her, which causes a scandal in Rome and emboldens his political rival Octavian (Roddy McDowall), who launches an invasion fleet to Egypt. In a fierce battle, Octavian’s forces defeat Antony at Actium, near Greece. Wrongly informed that Cleopatra is dead, Antony takes his own life—an act that leads Cleopatra to do the same.

## Off-screen drama [...] Cleopatra, however, was not without its merits. The visuals were impressive, and the acting by Burton and Harrison was outstanding; the latter earned an Academy Award nomination. Taylor’s interpretation of Cleopatra, however, was not as praised, with some calling her performance melodramatic.

## Production notes and credits

## Cast

## Academy Award nominations (\ denotes win) [...] Cleopatra was a troubled production with a background story that dwarfed any on-screen action. Ineptly produced and prone to disaster, the film experienced shooting delays, location changes, script rewrites, and director changes (Rouben Mamoulian was replaced by Joseph L. Mankiewicz). Adding to the drama was the affair between Burton and Taylor (who were both married to other people at the time) and the resulting media frenzy. Although the scandal helped generate huge interest in the movie—Cleopatra was among the highest-grossing films of 1963—the studio was unable to recoup its massive production budget.
